beginner: Plum likes a deep soil that drains well, from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam. Good drainage matters most, because plum roots do not like sitting in wet ground and can rot if they stay soggy. Of the common home fruit trees, plum is a little more forgiving of heavier ground than peach is, especially European types on a tolerant rootstock, but standing water is still the thing to avoid. If your soil is heavy clay that holds water, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the wettest layer. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
seasoned: Plum wants a deep, well-drained soil ranging from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam; drainage is the priority, since Prunus roots will not tolerate prolonged wet feet. Plum is somewhat more tolerant of heavier ground than peach, particularly European cultivars on a heavy-soil-tolerant rootstock such as Marianna or Myrobalan, but chronically saturated soil still invites crown and root rot. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above the perched water table. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

beginner: Plum grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Plum does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Do not overdo the nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much pushes soft, leafy growth that draws aphids and disease. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils. Go easy on nitrogen: plums push vigorous shoots readily, and lush, succulent growth is more prone to aphids, bacterial canker, and black knot, and never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard plums. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard plums; a young tree that is not making about a foot of new growth a year can take a spring nitrogen boost, but a vigorous tree needs little. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.

beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 8 to 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing strongly, with lots of long new shoots, give it less, not more.
seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 8 to 10 cups for a mature tree. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree making 8 to 15 inches of new wood a year is fed about right, and one growing faster than that needs less nitrogen, not more.

beginner: Whether a plum needs a companion tree is really a pollination question, and it depends on the type. European plums (like Stanley, Italian prune, and damson) are mostly self-fruitful, so one tree makes fruit on its own. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) usually need a second, different Japanese variety blooming nearby to set a good crop. Beyond that, the things that matter for a tree are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps the tree settle in. One thing to avoid is planting a plum near other wild or neglected plums and cherries, because those spread black knot, the black warty branch disease, to your tree.
seasoned: For a plum, the key interaction is pollination, and it splits by type: European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson) are largely self-fruitful and fruit alone, while Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley, and most others) are self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time. The other interactions that matter are about the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since a young tree competes poorly with grass for water and nitrogen. The site rule to respect is inoculum: do not plant near wild, ornamental, or neglected Prunus (chokecherry, wild plum, purple-leaf plum), which are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot.

beginner: On small developing plums, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall, and it is the usual reason for wormy plums.
seasoned: Small developing fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is one of the most common causes of wormy backyard plums.

beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio, which is named for this very crop. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit and later drop to the ground.
seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle and a signature pest of its namesake crop. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside, then drop to pupate in the soil.

beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the cool early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.

beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.

beginner: In spring the new leaves at the shoot tips curl up tightly, and if you unroll one you find little green or waxy-gray insects, aphids, packed inside. They leave a sticky shine (called honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold. A bad early attack curls the leaves and slows the new growth.
seasoned: In spring, new leaves at the shoot tips pucker and curl tightly around colonies of small soft-bodied aphids (leaf curl plum aphid), while the pale, wax-dusted mealy plum aphid clusters on the undersides of leaves. Both excrete honeydew that turns leaves shiny and sticky and grows black sooty mold; heavy early infestations stunt shoots and can distort young fruit.

beginner: Two kinds of aphids that live on plum: one curls the new leaves, and the other is a pale, waxy gray one. They spend the winter as eggs near the buds, then multiply fast on the tender spring growth before flying off to other summer plants.
seasoned: Two aphids specific to plum: the leaf curl plum aphid (Brachycaudus helichrysi), which curls the spring foliage, and the mealy plum aphid (Hyalopterus pruni), whitish with a mealy wax coat. Both overwinter as eggs near the buds, build up on new spring growth, then migrate to summer hosts (leaf curl plum aphid to plants in the aster family, mealy plum aphid to reeds and cattails).

beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful bugs usually clean aphids up by early summer, so avoid harsh sprays that kill those helpers too. Blast the colonies off with a hard spray of water, and for a bad case use insecticidal soap or a light horticultural oil on the curled shoots. A dormant oil spray in late winter kills the overwintering eggs.
seasoned: Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, parasitic wasps) usually bring aphids under control by early summer, so protect them by not spraying broad insecticides. A strong jet of water knocks colonies off, and narrow-range horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the affected shoots helps in a heavy infestation. A dormant or delayed-dormant oil spray targets the overwintering eggs.

beginner: Go easy on spring feeding, since lush new growth attracts aphids. Keep ants off the trunk (they protect aphids) with a sticky band, and leave the helpful bugs alone. If aphids come back every year, a dormant oil spray in late fall or winter is the best prevention.
seasoned: Avoid heavy spring nitrogen, which pushes the soft flush aphids favor. Keep ants (which farm aphids for honeydew and drive off predators) off the trunk with a sticky band, and preserve natural enemies. A late-fall or dormant oil where aphids are a chronic problem is the most effective single measure.

beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. The peachtree borer, which also attacks plums, leaves a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so catch this early.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Plums, like other stone fruit, are a host. A heavily infested young tree loses vigor as the larvae girdle the inner bark; several borers in one trunk can kill a newly planted tree in a season.

beginner: The larvae (young grub stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly by day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest.
seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose day-flying adults are wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; larvae tunnel in the inner bark at and just below the soil line. Trees stressed by winter injury, mechanical wounds, or bacterial canker are attacked first.

beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back.
seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire. Keep the trunk base free of wounds.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury (the wounds that draw egg-laying females), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum.

beginner: Little gray, round, hard bumps crust over the bark of twigs and branches, and the fruit can get small reddish spots where the scales feed. A bad infestation makes the bark look ashy and can kill off twigs and branches, weakening the tree.
seasoned: Tiny gray, circular, hard-shelled scales encrust the bark of twigs and branches, sometimes so densely the bark looks ashy; feeding sites on fruit show as small red-purple haloed spots. Heavy infestations kill twigs and whole limbs from the top down and weaken the tree over a few seasons.

beginner: An armored scale insect called San Jose scale. After the tiny young 'crawlers' settle down, they stay put under a hard shell and suck sap, with several generations a year. Only the crawler stage moves around and can be targeted.
seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect. Immobile once settled, it feeds on sap under a waxy shell and passes several overlapping generations a year; crawlers (the mobile young stage) are the only vulnerable window and spread the infestation along the branches.

beginner: The main control is a thorough spray of horticultural oil in late winter while the tree is leafless, coating all the bark to smother the scales. During the season, helpful insects keep light infestations down. Prune out and destroy branches that are heavily crusted with scale.
seasoned: A thorough dormant or delayed-dormant application of horticultural oil, wetting all the bark, smothers overwintering scales and is the mainstay of home control. In-season, natural enemies (tiny parasitic wasps, predatory beetles) suppress light infestations; prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.

beginner: Prune for good airflow, use a dormant oil spray in areas where scale has shown up before, and check any new trees you buy, since scale often hitches in on nursery stock. Avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful insects.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and well pruned so airflow is good, apply dormant oil where scale has appeared before, and inspect incoming nursery stock, since scale often arrives on new trees. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

beginner: Hard, black, warty lumps (called knots) grow along the twigs and branches, anywhere from an inch to six inches or more long. They start as a soft olive-green swelling one year and turn coal-black and hard the next. The branch beyond a knot often wilts and dies, and a badly infected tree gets stunted and gnarled. Black knot is the classic plum disease, the one to learn to recognize.
seasoned: Hard, black, elongated, warty swellings (knots) grow along twigs and branches, from an inch to six inches or more long, girdling and eventually killing the wood beyond them. A new gall starts as an inconspicuous olive-green, corky swelling one year, then hardens and turns coal-black by the second. Leaves on knotted branches may wilt and die, and a heavily infected tree becomes stunted and misshapen. This is the signature disease of plum.

beginner: A fungus (Apiosporina morbosa) that lives in the black knots over winter, on your tree and on any wild plums or cherries nearby. In cool, wet spring weather it shoots out spores that infect the new green shoots. You will not see anything the first year; the knot swells the next year and turns black the year after.
seasoned: The fungus Apiosporina morbosa (formerly Dibotryon morbosum). It overwinters in the galls on the tree and on nearby wild or ornamental Prunus, and in cool, wet spring weather releases spores that infect the new green shoots. Infection is invisible the first season; the gall swells the following year and blackens the year after, so the disease runs on a roughly two-year cycle.

beginner: Cutting the knots out is the main fix, and when you do it matters: prune in late winter while the tree is bare, before it starts growing in spring. Cut each knot off 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, into clean wood, because the fungus reaches farther than you can see. Carry the cut pieces away and burn, bury, or bag them so they cannot re-infect the tree, and wipe your pruners with rubbing alcohol between cuts.
seasoned: Pruning is the core control, and timing is everything: in the dormant season, before growth resumes (before about April 1), cut out every knot, making the cut 3 to 4 inches below the visible gall into clean wood, since the fungus extends beyond what you can see. Remove the prunings from the area and burn, bury, or bag them, and disinfect tools between cuts. On a scaffold too valuable to remove, cut the gall out to healthy wood. A protective fungicide on the new shoots in early spring supports the pruning where pressure is high.

beginner: Check the tree every winter and cut out any knots before spring, when they spread. Just as important, clean up or remove wild plums, chokecherries, and neglected ornamental plums nearby, because they keep re-infecting your tree. Some plum varieties resist black knot better than others, so ask when you buy, but cutting the knots out each year is the habit that matters most.
seasoned: Scout and prune out knots every dormant season before they can release spores, and deal with the reservoir: remove or clean up wild plum, chokecherry, and neglected ornamental Prunus within range, which sustain the disease. Choosing a less-susceptible cultivar and keeping the tree open and vigorous both help, but annual knot removal is the non-negotiable habit.

beginner: At bloom, infected flowers go limp and brown, and small gummy dead patches can form on the nearby twigs. As the plums ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on the surface. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard, dried mummy that hangs on the tree.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and turn brown, and the infection can run back into the twig to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, brown circular spots appear and spread fast, sometimes rotting a whole plum within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a mummy that clings to the tree or drops.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia fructicola. It survives the winter in dried mummy fruit and in dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers. Those flower infections later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, humid, wet weather makes it spread fast, and any break in the skin lets it in.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia fructicola. It overwinters in mummified fruit (whether hanging in the canopy or fallen) and in twig cankers; spores released at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet conditions drive rapid spread, and any skin break (curculio scar, hail, cracking) is an entry point.

beginner: The main control is cleanup: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, since these hold the spores. If the weather is wet during bloom, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. As soon as you see a plum rotting, pick it and throw it away, and thin the fruit so plums are not touching.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out gummy twig cankers, because these are the spore sources. During a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Once fruit is rotting, pick and dispose of it promptly, and thin fruit so plums do not touch, which slows spread through a cluster.

beginner: Cleanup all year prevents most of the damage: never leave dried mummies on the tree over winter, pick up dropped fruit, and prune so the tree is open and the plums dry fast after rain. Keep pests like plum curculio in check, since their wounds let rot in. Pick fruit on time, handle it gently, and chill it soon after picking.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies on the tree over winter, remove dropped and thinned fruit, and keep the canopy open with good pruning so fruit dries quickly after rain. Control plum curculio and other pests whose wounds open the door, harvest promptly, handle fruit gently, and cool it soon after picking.

beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn dark and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety, and Japanese plums are often more affected than European ones.
seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown to purple-black and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks develop on the skin, downgrading the crop. Susceptibility varies sharply by cultivar, and Japanese plums are often hit harder than European.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up when there are other susceptible plum or peach trees close by. The spots can look like spray damage.
seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up where susceptible plum, peach, and related trees grow nearby. Symptoms are sometimes mistaken for spray injury or nutrient problems.

beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and the canopy open so it shrugs off the damage.
seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.

beginner: The best prevention is the variety you pick. Choosing a plum known to resist or tolerate bacterial spot avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. Good airflow, going easy on nitrogen, and a healthy tree also help.
seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar at planting; this is largely a variety decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, avoiding excess nitrogen, and tree vigor reduce severity.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Sandy soil dries out faster and needs watering more often; heavier soil stays wet longer. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water on a deep-and-infrequent rhythm rather than a little every day: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in the heat of summer, always adjusted for rain and soil type. A sandy soil dries faster and needs more frequent soaks; a heavier soil holds longer. Through winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give the tree a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a quick splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. Deep soaks help the tree grow deep roots that handle dry spells.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so the moisture reaches the full depth of the root zone, rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries the tree through dry spells.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots using a drip line or a soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot take hold, so put the water on the soil, not on the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness and feeds brown rot and bacterial spot, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill. That is because waterlogged roots cannot breathe and start to rot. In plum, soil that stays wet can also bring on crown and root rot, which often kills the tree. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a generally declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate and rot. In stone fruit, chronically wet soil also invites crown and root rot, which is often fatal and rarely reversible once advanced. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the plums are sizing up makes small, shriveled fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a prolonged dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its plums poorly, leaving them small and prone to shriveling even though the tree itself survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the plums are setting and sizing up, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. This is exactly when steady watering pays off in bigger, better plums.
seasoned: From fruit set through the final swell, do not let the tree dry out. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and helps prevent the shriveling that dry stress causes.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years to get established. Older trees can handle some dry spells, but the plums come out small if the tree gets too dry.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot and bacterial spot. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature trees are moderately drought-tolerant but size fruit poorly under stress.

beginner: The most important time to keep the tree watered is the last few weeks before harvest, when the plums do most of their growing. If the tree runs dry then, the fruit stays small and watering later will not fix it. The few weeks right after bloom matter too. If you ever have to cut back on water, the safest time is the middle of the season, when the pits are hardening.
seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell, roughly the last 3 to 5 weeks before harvest, when cell expansion adds most of the fruit's final size. Water stress then causes irreversible loss of size and can leave plums small and prone to shriveling. Early rapid growth just after bloom is also sensitive; mild stress during pit hardening (mid-season) is the most tolerable time to ease off if water is limited.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoor conditions) does not apply to plum. You plant it bare-root and dormant, in late winter or early spring, rather than as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to plum. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter or early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.

beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.
seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two beforehand to rehydrate them. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree so the graft union (that swollen joint near the base of the trunk) sits 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not add fertilizer to the planting hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake only if the site is windy.

beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice mixed in for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil that stays wet. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity stone-fruit roots demand; plum will not tolerate a mix that holds water against the crown. Skip native garden soil in a pot, which compacts and drains poorly under irrigation.

beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. beginner: A plum is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and comes in two main types that act differently. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) are juicier for fresh eating but bloom early (so frost is more of a risk) and usually need a second, different Japanese plum nearby to set fruit. Plums take steady work: prune every winter (more gently than a peach), cut out black knot (a black branch disease), thin off extra fruit so the rest grow big, and plant in a sunny, well-drained spot away from frost pockets. Either way plum asks for real commitment: annual dormant pruning (lighter than a peach), diligent black knot removal, early fruit thinning, and a frost-aware, well-drained site. Given that care, a backyard plum rewards you with tree-ripe fruit far better than the store.

beginner: A plum is ripe when it shows full color, has a natural dusty coating on the skin (that is normal, not a problem), gives a little when you press gently, and comes off the branch with an easy pull. Within a type, cross-pollinating varieties must have overlapping bloom to set fruit, so a Japanese plum and its pollenizer need to flower at the same time.

seasoned: Plum splits along species lines here. The low-chill Japanese plums, needing only a few hundred chill hours, are a desert Southwest classic and fit the warm St. George core, where Washington County Extension lists plum among the fruits that do well at low elevation. The high-chill European prune plums need more winter cold than the valley floor banks and are a poorer fit. The dry air keeps disease low; a late frost on the early bloom and steady irrigation through the hot season, not chill or brown rot, are the defining concerns.
